rituals.name: BIRTH CATCHER
rituals.plain:
Your next thought is arriving without an appointment. Catch it at the door.
Rest your attention on one ordinary point. When a thought turns up by itself, catch its very first moment.
Don't choose the thought that arrives.
Name its shape: a word, picture, memory, plan or sensation. Then let it move on.

rituals.name: DEATH CATCHER
rituals.plain:
Even this thought has an exit. No farewell speech needed.
Let one manageable thought stay until it fades by itself. Notice the first beat when it is no longer there.
Don't replace it with another thought on purpose.
Stay with that gap for just one beat.

rituals.name: FIRST-WORD TRAP
rituals.plain:
One word gets in. Its entourage can wait.
When your inner voice starts, hold just its first word for two beats. Leave the sentence unfinished.
Let the second word wait for this tiny round.
If a picture arrives instead, wait for its first caption word.

rituals.name: NO-SEQUEL
rituals.plain:
That thought is demanding a sequel. Did we order one?
When it finishes, spend five seconds letting any explanation, defence, prediction or replay go without adding the next line.
Let the first thought have its whole sentence.
A genuinely unrelated thought is welcome.

rituals.name: QUEUE MASTER
rituals.plain:
Your thoughts have forgotten how queues work. Tickets, please.
Picture numbered tickets for the competing thoughts. Give the lowest number three beats of attention while the others wait.

Thoughts may exist while the window is closed.
Do two cycles.

rituals.name: UNFINISHED MAGNET

Stop one step before completion.
Don't complete the count during the observation window.

rituals.name: EVIDENCE LINE

Place the key observations from the situation into a small imagined grid. Try to trace one straight horizontal, vertical, or diagonal line that genuinely supports the conclusion.
No skipping between unrelated cues to complete the pattern.
If support requires jumping around the grid, mark the conclusion as PATCHED rather than LINED.

The target word stays the same across both trials.
Compare ease or immediacy, not correctness.

rituals.name: LETTER WEIGHT
rituals.plain:
Turn the loaded word into letter values. Drama, meet arithmetic.
Choose the most charged word in the thought. Convert its letters to alphabet positions and add them into one number. Hold the sentence with that number replacing the word.
The proposition stays available; only the keyword loses readable language.
Notice what remains understandable and what emotional force disappears when the label can't be read.

rituals.name: PERSPECTIVE TRANSPOSE
rituals.plain:
Swap the rows and columns of the story. The social spreadsheet can turn around.
Imagine a tiny matrix: people on rows, possible meanings on columns. Notice where your current interpretation sits. Now transpose it so meanings become rows and people become columns.
The observations remain fixed while person and interpretation change roles.
Ask whether the same interpretation would be assigned as readily to another person with the same observable behaviour.

rituals.name: CROWD MIRROR
rituals.plain:
Do you expect everyone to pick what you picked? Your opinion isn't a population survey.
Choose tea or coffee. Then estimate, out of 100 random adults, how many would make the same choice. Notice whether your own preference pulls the estimate upward.
Preference and prevalence are two separate answers.
Keep the population estimate separate from whether your own choice is better.

rituals.name: SOUND SNAP

Keep the three sounds distinct until the blend.
Don't add any extra sound between them.

rituals.name: MEANING MELT
rituals.plain:
Repeat one ordinary word and hear its sound change. The word may lose its serious suit.
Pick the neutral word WINDOW. Repeat it internally around fifteen times at a quick, even pace. When the repetitions end, check whether the sound briefly feels stranger than its meaning.
Use one neutral word and keep the pace steady.
Avoid explaining the word while repeating it.

rituals.name: MENTAL STATIC THRESHOLD
rituals.plain:
How much imagined static masks one inner word? The narrator has competition.
Hear one neutral word internally with faint imagined static behind it. Increase only the static until the word becomes just unreadable by ear.
Raise static gradually; don't lower the word's own volume.
Stop once the first clear loss of intelligibility.

rituals.name: CAUSE SWITCH
rituals.plain:
If the supposed cause changed, what should happen? The theory needs a test drive.
Use a harmless example: coffee drinking and alertness rise together. Imagine actively setting coffee to zero while sleep and time of day stay the same. Ask what each causal story predicts.
An intervention changes the candidate cause rather than merely observing it.
Don't treat correlation alone as the intervention result.

rituals.name: RULE BOUNDARY
rituals.plain:
Where does this rule actually apply? It doesn't have global jurisdiction.
Take 'I must...' and find the exact contexts where it's genuinely useful or required.
Name context boundaries.
Everything else outside.

rituals.name: CONTRAPOSITIVE
rituals.plain:
Turn the rule around without changing its logic. Grammar isn't the same as proof.
Use: 'If it's a square, it has four sides.' Form the contrapositive: 'If it doesn't have four sides, it's not a square.'
Reverse the direction and negate both parts.
Don't confuse it with simply reversing the original rule.

rituals.name: MONTY SWITCH
rituals.plain:
New information arrived. Your first choice doesn't need a loyalty card.
Pick Door 1 from three doors. The host, who knows the prize, opens Door 3 and shows no prize. Decide whether to stay with Door 1 or switch to Door 2.
The host always reveals a losing door you did not choose.
Track where the original 2/3 probability mass can go after the host's forced reveal.

rituals.name: INFERENCE STEP COUNT
rituals.plain:
How many jumps connect that fact to the conclusion? Your brain has been doing parkour.
Use a mild example: FACT='They replied late.' CONCLUSION='They are angry with me.' Name every extra assumption needed to get from the fact to the conclusion and count them.
Each unsupported leap counts as one step.
Don't decide whether the conclusion is true; count only the bridge steps.
